summary:
New South Wales administers its own discrimination, document, facilities and custody rules inside Australia's national framework. Birth certificates and driver licences are issued by the state; marriage and passports remain national matters and are carried at the national level.

The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 has covered transgender status since 1996 and prohibits discrimination in employment, public education, goods and services, banking, health care, property and nightclubs. Section 16 of the Mental Health Act 2007 states expressly that sexual orientation and gender identity are not mental illnesses. Exemptions within the same statute cut against that protection: sport and broadly-based religious exemptions in non-public schools permit discrimination on grounds including sex and gender, which allows transgender people to be barred from female sports categories and students and teachers to be expelled from religiously-run schools.

Since 1 July 2025 a person born or adopted in New South Wales can change the sex recorded on their birth certificate without surgery, on application, with a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known for at least a year and a fee of $73. There is no cap on the number of sex changes, unlike name changes, which are limited to once every 12 months and three in a lifetime. Until 30 June 2025 sexual reassignment surgery and a $153 fee were legally required, with no disclosure of the change on the new certificate, and the requirement to divorce before changing sex was abolished in June 2018. In April 2014 the High Court of Australia held that the law permits registration of a change of sex to a non-specific descriptor, in the case of Norrie May-Welby, and since March 2022 birth certificates carrying no gender or sex entry have been available for people born or adopted in the state.

Conversion practices are criminalised. The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025: practices causing substantial mental or physical harm carry up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years. Anti-Discrimination NSW has been able to investigate complaints from 4 April 2025, with civil referral pathways available. The legislation passed unamended on 22 March 2024 by 22 votes to 4 in the upper house and retains limited religious and parental exemptions, including an exception for religious sermons.

Publicly threatening or inciting violence is a criminal offence. The Crimes Amendment (Publicly Threatening and Inciting Violence) Act 2018 passed both houses unanimously in June 2018, repealed the state's vilification provisions and created an offence carrying up to three years' imprisonment, in force from 13 August 2018.

Facilities: Sydney City Council adopted a gender-neutral bathrooms policy in April 2023. It governs council facilities; the sources record no equivalent state-wide requirement.

Custody: since 1996 New South Wales prisoner protocols and guidelines have permitted transgender prisoners who have had sexual reassignment surgery to be housed in female prisons for protection. In November 2024 the state government granted an undisclosed settlement to a transgender individual held in a male prison.

Violence: in 2021 Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines visiting Australia, was killed in Wagga Wagga, New South Wales; the perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month custodial term. The most recent documented instance of fatal violence against a trans person in this record is that 2021 case; no later instance is documented.

Official posture: in October 2020 the New South Wales Legislative Assembly carried a unanimous, non-binding, bipartisan lower-house motion calling for human rights, dignity and respect for transgender individuals.
tangentialFactors:
A judicial inquiry into LGBTIQ hate crimes was announced in November 2021 and began work in November 2022, examining 88 deaths of gay men between 1970 and 2000; NSW Police were called to give evidence in December 2022. The inquiry concerns gay men rather than trans people, and no trans-specific findings or outcomes from it appear in the sources.

The state banned Nazi symbols under the Crimes Act 1900, assented 19 August 2022 and effective immediately, a measure the sources describe as intended to protect the LGBTIQ community.

A government hate crimes bill concerning gay and bi men, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, was put forward in March 2026 and has not been debated in either house; no enactment is recorded.

The provocation defence at common law, known as the gay panic defence, was abolished unanimously in May 2014 and took effect in June 2014, removing a route by which a killing could be reduced to manslaughter on the basis of the victim's sexuality or gender presentation.

Private consensual sex between men has been legal in New South Wales since 1984, with the age of consent equalised at 16 for all forms of sex in May 2003; the Criminal Records Amendment (Historical Homosexual Offences) Act 2014, passed unanimously on 23 October 2014 and effective 24 November 2014, allows expungement of historical private consensual adult gay male convictions, and a formal NSW Government apology followed in June 2024 on the 40th anniversary of decriminalisation.
localsOnly:
766 sex changes had been recorded on New South Wales birth certificates by September 2025 under the process that took effect on 1 July 2025.

Inner West Council in Sydney voted to approve transgender health leave for its staff. The policy has not taken effect because it requires the signature of the local government minister; whether it has since been signed is not recorded in the sources.

Residents who change the sex on a birth certificate face no equivalent restriction on repeat changes, while name changes remain limited to once every 12 months and three in a lifetime.

Transgender students and staff in non-public schools remain exposed to the sport and religious exemptions in the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977, which permit exclusion on grounds including sex and gender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity is a listed ground in the state's current criminal provision against publicly threatening or inciting violence is unresolved. The sources give the 2018 Act's title, its unanimous passage, its commencement date of 13 August 2018 and its three-year maximum, but do not state the grounds it covers.

No charging or prosecution data appears for offences under the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 since 4 April 2025, nor for the 2018 publicly threatening and inciting violence offence. Complaint volumes received by Anti-Discrimination NSW under the conversion-practices regime are likewise not sourced.

The status of the March 2026 government hate crimes bill is unresolved: it is recorded as not yet debated in either house, with no later legislative step documented.

Whether the Inner West Council transgender health leave has since been signed into effect is not sourced.

No data is available on how the prisoner-housing protocol has been applied in practice, and the terms of the November 2024 settlement with a transgender prisoner held in a male prison are undisclosed.

The sources record no state-wide facilities mandate for gender-neutral toilets beyond the April 2023 Sydney City Council policy, and no later council or state adoption is documented.
